hero.title: Static, const, and readonly
intro.0: Not every value belongs to a single object. Some behaviour lives on the type itself, some values are fixed the moment you write them, and some are set once when an object is built and then never change. You write each kind and run it.
task.1.title: A helper that needs no instance
task.1.context:
Some behaviour does not belong to any one object - it belongs to the **type**. Doubling a number needs no particular zoo; any caller can just ask the type to do it. A `static` method lives on the class, so you call it as `Zoo.Double(3)` - no `new`, no instance.

Give `Zoo` a `static int Double(int n)` that returns `n` twice.
task.1.goal.0: Give `Zoo` a `static int Double(int n)` that returns `n + n`.
task.1.goal.1: `Main` calls `Zoo.Double(3)` on the type - no `new` - so the output is `6`.
task.2.title: A value that never changes
task.2.context:
A dog has four legs - that number is fixed, and nothing in the program should ever change it. A `const` is a named value set once, at the point you write it, and never again. You give it a clear name instead of scattering the bare number `4` through your code.

Give `Herd` a `const int LegsPerCow = 4` and a `int Legs(int cows)` that returns the total number of legs.
task.2.goal.1: Give `Herd` a `int Legs(int cows)` that returns `cows * LegsPerCow`.
task.3.title: Set once, then fixed
task.3.context:
Sometimes a value is not known until you build the object, but once set it should never change. A cat gets its name when it is created, and it keeps that name for life. A `readonly` field can be assigned in the constructor and nowhere else - the compiler stops any later reassignment.

Give `Cat` a `readonly` name field, set in the constructor, and a `Name()` that returns it.
task.3.goal.3: `Main` builds `new Cat("Milo")` and prints `Name()`, so the output is `Milo`.
task.4.title: One value the whole type shares
task.4.context:
Each `new` object gets its own fields. But sometimes you want one value shared across every instance - a tally that all objects add to. A `static` field belongs to the type, not to any one object, so there is a single copy. Count each sheep as it is built, and every sheep sees the same total.

Give `Sheep` a `static` counter that goes up by one in the constructor, read through a `static int Count()`.
task.4.goal.1: In the constructor, add one to `_count`.
task.4.goal.2: Give `Sheep` a `static int Count()` that returns `_count`.
task.4.goal.3: `Main` builds two sheep, then prints `Sheep.Count()`, so the output is `2`.
task.5.title: What you learned
task.5.context: Four ways a value or a method can belong to the type itself, or be fixed for good.
task.5.summaryIntro: Not everything belongs to a single object. Some behaviour and data sit on the type, and some values never change. You wrote each one by hand:
task.5.summaryItems.0.title: A static method -
task.5.summaryItems.0.text: behaviour that needs no instance; you call `Zoo.Double(3)` on the type, with no `new`.
task.5.summaryItems.1.title: A const -
task.5.summaryItems.1.text: a named value fixed where you write it - `const int LegsPerCow = 4` - so the number has a name and can never change.
task.5.summaryItems.2.title: A readonly field -
task.5.summaryItems.2.text: set once in the constructor and never again; a `Cat` keeps the name it was built with for life.
task.5.summaryItems.3.title: A static field -
task.5.summaryItems.3.text: one copy shared by every instance; a `static` counter lets each new sheep add to the same total.
task.5.summaryClose: The idea is portable: `const` and `readonly` say a value will not change, and `static` says something belongs to the type rather than to one object. Other languages spell these differently, but the three ideas are the same everywhere.
